Check that Arnesen et al.'s one-turn models were trained with the same procedure as the two-turn models (Appendix G says identical procedures)

out.rationale: An explicit 'aligns with the findings of' statement: Arnesen et al. state that judges being equivalently accurate on one- and two-turn debates and consultancies aligns with the findings of Khan et al. (2024) and Kenton et al. (2024), who observed a similar phenomenon. No record of Khan et al.'s paper states the turn-count result, so the link is paper-level; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result. That record's claim (76% and 88% judge accuracy, and gains from optimising debaters for persuasiveness) is not what the passage aligns with, so the passage gives no evidence for it. Equal accuracy on one- and two-turn debates and consultancies does not bear on whether debate helps judges above the naive baselines of 48% and 60%, and the target states no turn-count result, so neither bears on the other's claim and the link proposes only SHARES_TOPIC rather than ADDRESSES or SUPPORTS.
out.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: Judge accuracy in LLM-judged QuALITY debates; the source asks whether it changes with the number of debate turns, and the target record states no turn-count result

text: The authors report that their judge is equally accurate on one-turn and two-turn debates and consultancies, and state that this aligns with a similar phenomenon observed by Khan et al. (2024). They take it as further evidence that judges are not sensitive to second-speech refutations.
title: Arnesen et al. find one- and two-turn debates are judged equally well, as Khan et al. observed
